description: We are a team of Computer Engineering and Computer Science students from Ukraine. Ready to solve space challenges together!
summary:
Lunar Horizon Navigator is an interactive web application built to help mission planners, scientists, and educators rapidly evaluate and compare lunar landing sites, with a special focus on the challenging terrain of the Moon’s South Pole.
Traditional tools like JPL Horizons, Moon Trek, and Quickmap offer deep scientific data, but switching between complex interfaces makes rapid scenario comparison difficult when launch schedules change. Powered by a modern React and TypeScript frontend alongside a FastAPI backend, our platform integrates lunar ephemeris and topography datasets into one intuitive dashboard.
Users can explore preset or custom lunar coordinates, scrub through interactive timelines to visualize Sun and Earth positions relative to the local horizon, assess power and Direct-to-Earth communication windows, and compare multiple landing scenarios side-by-side.
details:
What It Does & How It Works
Lunar Landing Site Navigator is a web app that makes it easier to check and compare landing spots on the Moon, especially near the South Pole. Existing NASA tools have great data, but they can be slow and confusing when you just want to quickly test different dates or locations. In our app, you pick a landing site (from a preset list or by typing your own coordinates), choose a start date and mission length, and immediately see where the Sun and Earth are in the sky relative to the local horizon.
Main Features
  • Sky & Horizon View: Shows the path of the Sun and Earth so you can see when mountains or crater edges block them.
  • Time Slider: Lets you move hour-by-hour through the mission to see how lighting and Earth visibility change over time.
  • Power & Comm Stats: Calculates how much sunlight and Direct-to-Earth communication time a site gets, shows countdowns to sunset/Earthset, and lets you download the data as a CSV file.
  • Site Comparison: Lets you put two or more landing sites (or different dates) side by side to quickly see which option is better if a launch gets delayed.
How We Built It
We used Python and FastAPI for the backend to calculate the Sun and Earth angles and serve the data, and React, TypeScript, and Vite for the frontend interface and charts. When building the logic, we focused on how the Moon has no atmosphere—meaning the horizon depends strictly on the local terrain—and how small changes in location or date at the South Pole can completely change sunlight availability.
Why It Matters
Our goal was to take complex orbital and terrain data (from JPL Horizons, Moon Trek / LOLA, and Quickmap) and turn it into a clean, easy-to-use tool that helps both mission planners and students quickly understand lunar landing trade-offs.
